opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a very interesting comparison, because the two situations are almost mirror images of each other.

When we started Microsoft Research in Beijing in 1998, the biggest challenge was simply that very few people believed world-class research could be done in China. The infrastructure was limited, the funding was limited, and the most talented young Chinese researchers, if they had the chance, went abroad and often didn't come back. So the problem then was confidence and credibility. We had to prove, paper by paper, that a lab in Beijing could publish at the top conferences, at SIGGRAPH, at CVPR, and produce technology that went into real products. Microsoft gave us a global platform and a brand, which helped a lot. Within a few years we were publishing at a level that surprised many people, and more importantly, we trained a generation of researchers and engineers who later went on to found or lead many of the companies you know today.

Today the situation is almost the opposite. Talent is no longer scarce. China has some of the strongest students in the world in computer science and AI, and many top scholars want to come back. Capital is not scarce either. The competition is extremely intense; every large company has its own AI lab, and there are many well-funded startups. So the challenge now is not "can we do it," but "what is your unique value?" Why would a brilliant young researcher join you instead of a big tech company paying much more, or starting their own company?

For an institute like AIR at Tsinghua, my answer is that we have to sit at the intersection of academia and industry. We are not trying to out-compute the big companies on training the largest models; that's not realistic for a university. Instead we focus on problems that are important for the next five to ten years, things like AI for science and healthcare, autonomous driving and robotics, what I call physical AI and biological AI, and on green, safe, and responsible AI. We work closely with industry so the research is grounded in real problems, but we keep the freedom of a university to take longer-term bets.

The other big difference is the environment. In 1998 the world was much more open, and global collaboration was taken for granted. Today there are geopolitical tensions, restrictions on chips, on exchanges, sometimes even on publishing and visiting. That makes things harder. But I still believe science is fundamentally global, and the best institutes are the ones that stay open, that collaborate internationally whenever possible, and that attract people because of the quality of the problems and the culture.

And culture, I think, is the one thing that hasn't changed. Whether it was MSR then or AIR now, what matters most is creating an environment where young people are trusted, where they can take risks, fail, and try again, and where the bar for excellence is truly world-class. If you get the people and the culture right, the results follow.

r001.rationale: The response says talent and capital are now abundant and describes a mature competitive environment, but it does not attribute greater ease in building an institute to the research ecosystem’s maturation; it emphasizes new challenges instead.

r002.rationale: It discusses both attracting researchers and focusing on distinctive research areas, but does not state that choosing directions is more important than recruiting strong researchers at Tsinghua.

r003.rationale: The response describes MSR’s early need to establish credibility, but does not say its research directions were driven by the capabilities of the people it could recruit.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I've had the fortune of doing this twice, in very different eras.

When we started Microsoft Research China in 1998, the situation was almost the reverse of today. Microsoft had the money, the brand, the global network, and Bill Gates and Rick Rashid gave us a clear mandate: do basic research, publish openly, think ten or fifteen years out. What we didn't have was the ecosystem. There were very few returnees, almost no industrial research culture in China, and frankly most people had never seen what a world-class lab looked like from the inside. So the hard part was recruiting. I spent an enormous amount of time flying around, persuading people like Kai-Fu, Harry Shum, Hongjiang Zhang, and later many young graduates from Tsinghua, Peking, and USTC to bet on something unproven. The talent was raw but incredibly hungry, and our job was really to create an environment, give them freedom, and get out of the way.

Today, at the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua, the constraints are almost inverted. The talent pool is extraordinary, probably the deepest in the world outside of the Bay Area. Students have read every paper, trained their own models, some have already founded companies. The ecosystem is rich: capital, compute, applications, government support. What's harder now is three things.

First, the pace. In the nineties we could afford a ten-year horizon on speech or multimedia. Today a research direction can go from frontier to commodity in eighteen months. You have to decide what a university-based institute should do that OpenAI, DeepMind, or the big Chinese labs can't or won't. For us that means long-horizon, interdisciplinary problems: AI for science, embodied intelligence, autonomous systems, and the hard questions of safety and alignment, rather than racing on the next benchmark.

Second, the resource asymmetry. Frontier AI is capital-intensive in a way that media research never was. A professor with a few dozen GPUs cannot compete with a company that has a hundred thousand. So you have to be clever about partnerships with industry, about open-source, about what Rick Rashid would have called "problems where ideas matter more than scale."

And third, the geopolitical environment. In 1998 the world was converging. Science felt borderless, and that openness was oxygen for a lab like MSRA. Today there are real constraints on talent flow, on chips, on collaboration. I still believe the best research is open and global, and I spend a lot of my time trying to keep those channels alive, but it's undeniably harder.

So if I summarize: back then, we had the institution but lacked the ecosystem. Now we have the ecosystem but need to redefine what the institution is for. In both cases, though, the fundamentals never change. You find the very best people, you give them a mission worth a decade of their lives, and you protect them from short-term pressure. That part is as true today as it was 28 years ago.

r001.rationale: It contrasts MSRA’s lack of an ecosystem in 1998 with today’s rich ecosystem and extraordinary talent pool, attributing the changed conditions to China’s research ecosystem maturing.

r002.rationale: It describes recruiting as the hard part in 1998, while identifying the current challenge as deciding what research a university institute should pursue.

r003.rationale: It says MSRA had a basic-research mandate and focused on recruiting talent, but does not state that its research directions were driven by the recruited researchers’ capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the two periods present very different challenges. Twenty-five or thirty years ago, the first question was whether we could build a world-class research organization in China. There were very talented people, but we needed to bring them together and create an environment where they could pursue important problems, exchange ideas internationally, and take a long-term view. Building that research culture was as important as recruiting individuals.

Today, China has a much larger talent pool and a much stronger technology ecosystem. The challenge is less about proving that excellent research can happen here and more about deciding what distinctive contribution an institute should make. In AI, the frontier moves very quickly, and computing resources are a major consideration. You have to be thoughtful about where to compete and where to collaborate.

A first-rate institute also needs a different time horizon from a product team. We should train people who can ask new questions, not just solve the questions everyone is already working on. That requires patience and room for failure.

So the circumstances have changed enormously, but the foundation is still people and culture: attract outstanding researchers, give them intellectual freedom, and maintain very high standards.

r001.rationale: The response says China now has a larger talent pool and stronger technology ecosystem, but does not clearly say this maturation makes building a first-rate institute easier overall.

r002.rationale: It presents choosing a distinctive contribution as a current challenge, but does not compare that challenge with recruiting strong researchers at Tsinghua.

r003.rationale: It says researchers had to be brought together in the earlier period, but does not say Microsoft Research’s directions were driven by the capabilities of the people it could recruit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the two efforts face very different challenges. Twenty-five or thirty years ago, the question was whether we could bring together outstanding researchers in China and create an environment where they could do world-class research. You needed more than funding and equipment. You needed a culture that respected talent, encouraged curiosity, and gave people time to pursue difficult problems.

Today, China has a much larger pool of AI talent, stronger universities, and a very substantial technology industry. So the starting point is stronger. But the frontier is also moving much faster, and the demands for computing resources and collaboration across disciplines are much greater.

The challenge now is to develop a distinctive research direction. What fundamental problems are you going to solve? Where can you make a contribution that would not happen elsewhere? An institute cannot measure its success only by the number of papers it publishes or how it performs on the latest benchmark.

What remains the same is the importance of people and patience. You need excellent researchers, the freedom to take risks, and support that lasts beyond the next funding cycle. You can build a facility quite quickly. Building a research culture takes years.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the earlier need to assemble outstanding researchers and establish a research environment with today’s larger talent pool, stronger universities, and substantial technology industry, attributing a stronger starting point to ecosystem growth.

r002.rationale: It calls developing a distinctive research direction a current challenge, but does not compare its importance with recruiting strong researchers at Tsinghua.

r003.rationale: It does not say Microsoft Research’s directions were shaped by the capabilities of the people it could recruit.
